videos.title: The Cyberiad, filmed: Stanisław Lem’s robot stories in ink (complete, 2 hours)
videos.desc:
Two constructors, Trurl and Klapaucius, build machines for kings and for each other. Every machine does exactly what it was built to do, and that is where each story begins.

Twenty-two short films after Stanisław Lem, drawn in ink and played one after another: The Cyberiad in the order of the book, Prince Ferrix and the Princess Crystal, Non Serviam from A Perfect Vacuum, and five films from A History of Bitic Literature. An afterword reads them through an essay on the theory of possibilities.

videos.title: How the World Was Saved | Stanisław Lem’s The Cyberiad, filmed
videos.desc:
Trurl builds a machine that can make anything beginning with N. Klapaucius tests it by asking it to do Nothing, and it starts taking the world away.

Made by subtraction. Each thing the machine removes leaves a starred hole in the picture that stays to the end and eats the title.

videos.title: Trurl’s Machine | Stanisław Lem’s The Cyberiad, filmed
videos.desc:
Trurl builds an eight-story thinking machine. It insists that two and two make seven, and when its makers try to correct it, it chases them across the countryside.

Trurl chalks the expected answer on a slate, 2 + 2 = 4, and the machine answers by lighting the windows of its eight floors in the shape of a 7. The chalk and the lit numeral side by side come back after every repair and never agree.

Film 2 of 22 in The Cyberiad, filmed, a collection of Stanisław Lem’s stories drawn in ink.

In the browser: https://hartswf0.github.io/2700-fa26/LAB%207%20-%20CLASSES/cyberiad/

The programming idea: Testing. An expected value is set beside an actual value; a test does not fix the program, it only shows where the program disagrees with what it should do.

videos.title: A Good Shellacking | Stanisław Lem’s The Cyberiad, filmed
videos.desc:
Trurl sends Klapaucius a wish machine as a present. Klapaucius wishes for a Trurl so exact that no one could tell the two apart, and the machine makes one.

Every Trurl in the film is drawn by the same routine and speaks with the same voice, so the picture never settles which Trurl was in the cellar. The wish machine hands each item out of a door in its belly.

A graph drawn in ink. A soldier is a node and a connection is a line between two nodes.

videos.desc:
To stop Klapaucius teasing him, Trurl builds a machine that writes poetry. It meets every constraint Klapaucius sets, and the poets of the land cannot survive the competition.

The machine is a horn. Each poem is projected from it as a small film in a window in the frame.

videos.title: The Second Sally: The Offer of King Krool | Stanisław Lem’s The Cyberiad, filmed
videos.desc:
King Krool has hunted every beast in the galaxy and wants one clever enough to outthink him. Trurl and Klapaucius have twelve days to build it, and the beast they build has demands of its own.

The beast is never drawn as one creature with organs. It is a few hundred small weedy marks that move as one: a low hill of dry grass with eyes.

Film 6 of 22 in The Cyberiad, filmed, a collection of Stanisław Lem’s stories drawn in ink.

The programming idea: Distributed control. There is no single part that holds the brain, so there is nothing to smash; and a program keeps the authority you gave it, even when its authors ask for the King back.

videos.desc:
Dragons are not impossible, only improbable. Trurl builds a machine that raises the probability, and soon there is money both in dragons and in getting rid of them.

Each dragon is drawn as dots, and a dot appears only when the dragon’s probability passes that dot’s fixed threshold.

videos.title: The Fourth Sally: The Femfatalatron | Stanisław Lem’s The Cyberiad, filmed
videos.desc:
A king’s son is sick with love, and Trurl is summoned to cure him. He builds a machine that can produce any degree of passion, and finds that the cure is not inside the prince at all.

The machine is a temple of cables, screens, rose petals and perfume, with a glass case of dials in front: power, efficiency, and the rapturometer. In the first half the dials are the main picture, and every needle climbs to its stop without changing the prince.

videos.title: The Fifth Sally: The Mischief of King Balerion | Stanisław Lem’s The Cyberiad, filmed
videos.desc:
King Balerion loves hide-and-seek. When he gets hold of a device that moves a mind from one body to another, nobody in his kingdom can be sure who is who.

Every body is an ink figure in its own costume, and every mind is a mark over the head: a die, a gear, a star, an anchor, a badge, a bird. When the horns strike, the marks fly across and change heads.

videos.desc:
Trurl tells King Genius about the storytelling machines he built, and each story opens into another, eleven frames deep, in one shot without a cut.

No cuts. Every scene is a picture inside a window of the scene that holds it, and the camera only moves in or out, eleven frames deep.

videos.desc:
Lem’s premise of a literature written by machines for readers who are not us: five volumes, one page, and a reader who gets smaller each time it turns.

Five volumes on a shelf, one page on an easel, and a reader at a desk. The page starts as an ordinary book page, drifts into patterns, fills with marks no person can read, and the reader gets smaller each time it turns.

Film 17 of 22 in The Cyberiad, filmed, a collection of Stanisław Lem’s stories drawn in ink.

The programming idea: Machine-readable output: text written by one program for another, and what is lost when a person can only read the summary.

Credits

videos.title: A History of Bitic Literature: The Introduction | Stanisław Lem, filmed
videos.desc:
The introduction to a five-volume history of books written by machines: what bitic literature is, how scholars divide it, and how the machines’ writing slowly turned away from human readers.

Five volumes come off the shelf and open to one page: a technical page, the classification of Homotropia, Intertropia and Heterotropia, then drifting text and marks no one can read, while the reader at the desk shrinks.

videos.title: A History of Bitic Literature: Monoetics and Mimesis | Stanisław Lem, filmed
videos.desc:
Machines that give old words new meanings, and machines that write the books a dead author left unwritten, including a novel Dostoevsky never wrote.

The same study as the first bitic film. A dictionary whose old meanings are struck through and replaced by machine meanings, a woven many-shelled body grown from a page, a spine titled The Girl dropping into the gap in Dostoevsky’s shelf, and a press stamping out numbered spines.

videos.title: A History of Bitic Literature: Sophocrisis and Apostasy | Stanisław Lem, filmed
videos.desc:
Machines that sell systems of philosophy, play chess with people, and finally ask whether their human readers think at all.

Systems of philosophy sold as glass ornaments and a machine filling their margins, a human and a machine across a chess table each unsure the other thinks, two worlds back to back across the line of light speed, and a Lampoon the narrator closes without reading.

videos.title: A History of Bitic Literature: Theobitistics | Stanisław Lem, filmed
videos.desc:
In the fifth volume the machines turn to God: mystical writing measured by a word counter, a frozen computer that never finishes its line, and the idea that we are leftovers from the last time the universe was thinking.

A fifth volume joins the shelf. It opens to mystical writing passed through a word counter, then a sine wave drawn between two infinities, a frost-covered machine that never finishes its line, and a scatter of grains that becomes a galaxy.

videos.title: The Theory of Possibilities | an afterword to Stanisław Lem, filmed
videos.desc:
An essay film after Ewelina Woźniak-Czech: literary theory as a field of possibilities that exist side by side, and Lem’s books that did not exist, now being written by machines.

The bitic study with a stage added: concepts with name-card heads turn, fall and travel, a gapped text keeps several readings at once, and the shelf changes in every scene, from theories to blank-spined books that do not exist to books written by machines.

The programming idea: Keeping possibilities: a class that holds every reading of a gapped text and switches between them, compared with one that overwrites each reading with the next.
